title: Ace Swarm
description: Stream health, peers and network paths of an Ace Swarm stack.

list.name: stream
list.label: Stream
list.description: Every stream by name. A deleted stream stays while the dashboard's range covers its life.

list.name: Layout changes
list.expr: sum by (stream, name) (increase(aceswarm_pipeline_layout_changes_total[$__rate_interval]) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}) > 0

panels.title: Engines running
panels.description: Engine containers running now. Each enabled stream has an engine of its own, plus its hot standbys on other paths. With "One engine per path" on, each path has one shared engine instead, for all its streams and their standbys. Engines kept to retry a move, and shared engines that stay a while after their last stream left, count too, and so do both engines while streams move to a new one. From the container runtime, every ENGINE_STATS_SECONDS (15 s).

panels.title: Recoveries in range
panels.description: Recoveries that brought video back in the dashboard's range, over all streams: one each time a stream plays again after recovery steps (aceswarm_stream_recoveries_succeeded_total). The steps that brought no video back don't count: every step taken is in Recovery attempts per hour, in the collapsed row Recovery attempts.

panels.title: Who is watching what
panels.description: Players showing a stream full screen right now. A viewer is a random id the page makes up when it loads and keeps only in memory, so every visit is a new viewer; the device is a rough guess from the browser.

panels.title: What each viewer watched
panels.description: One lane per viewer and stream: when each player showed which stream.

panels.title: Delivering new frames

targets.expr: ((aceswarm_stream_up * on (stream) (1 + 2 * (max by (stream) (aceswarm_stream_standby{state="hot"}) or on (stream) 0 * aceswarm_stream_up)) + on (stream) 2 * aceswarm_stream_state{state="stale-source"}) or on (stream) max by (stream) (4 * (aceswarm_stream_info{enabled="false"} == 1))) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.description: High availability (blue): the stream plays (Live in the UI) and produces new video frames, and at least one hot standby on another path receives the live broadcast too, so a failover takes seconds. A standby is hot while it got data in the last 10 seconds and its live edge moves (aceswarm_stream_standby{state="hot"}). Delivering (green): the stream plays and produces new video frames (aceswarm_stream_up), with no hot standby. Waiting for source (dark red): the stream is stale-source, because its source's live edge has not moved for STALE_SOURCE_SECONDS (60 by default) or the engine serves the stream that far behind its live edge. No old video is published, and the stream retries until the broadcast is back. Disabled (grey): the stream was turned off (aceswarm_stream_info{enabled="false"}); it is no outage, and its time off does not count in Availability in range. Not delivering (red): every other state (starting, buffering, stalled, recovering, switching path or error). Only video from a source whose live edge moves counts, so a broadcast that stops shows as one outage: red, then dark red.

panels.title: Availability in range
panels.description: The share of the time each stream was enabled that it delivered new frames (aceswarm_stream_up), over the dashboard's range. The time a stream was disabled does not count; a stream disabled for the whole range is not listed.

panels.title: Recoveries per hour
panels.description: Recoveries that brought video back (aceswarm_stream_recoveries_succeeded_total): a stream counts one each time it plays again after recovery steps, under the last step that changed where it plays from: restart-pipeline, restart-engine, switch-path, or failover to a hot standby. A restart by hand counts as restart-engine, unless the stream was playing. The steps tried before that one don't count, nor do the tries of a stream that waits for a broadcast that is off: every step taken is in Recovery attempts per hour, in the collapsed row Recovery attempts below.

panels.title: Age of the last new frame
panels.description: Seconds since players could last get a new video frame of the stream. It keeps growing for as long as an enabled stream has no video, however many recovery steps that takes. A disabled stream has no value, and neither has a stream that was started and has not had video since (aceswarm_stream_last_frame_age_seconds).

panels.title: Pipeline frame rate
panels.description: Frames per second each stream's ffmpeg processes, as ffmpeg reports it: its average since that ffmpeg started. A new ffmpeg first reads what the engine has buffered, faster than real time, so its line starts high and falls to the stream's real frame rate. There is no line while no ffmpeg runs for the stream (aceswarm_pipeline_fps).

panels.title: Broadcast quiet for
panels.description: Seconds since each stream's broadcast last sent new data: since the live edge of a live session of the stream last moved (the newest data of the broadcast its engine knows of). It is about 0 while the stream plays. Past STALE_SOURCE_SECONDS (60 by default) the broadcast counts as stopped: the stream shows 'Waiting for source', nothing old is published, and it tries a new session from time to time. Those tries don't start the line over: it keeps growing until a session sees new data. A stream that never had a live session counts from when its first session saw a live edge. No value while the stream's session shows no live position: its output is played as it comes (aceswarm_stream_source_quiet_seconds).

panels.title: Live edge age (broadcaster's clock)
panels.description: Age of the newest data of each stream's broadcast that its engine knows of (livepos.last). It is stamped by the broadcaster's clock, which can be off, so a steady offset is no problem; one that keeps growing is a broadcast that stopped.

panels.title: Key frames only or every frame

targets.expr: max by (stream) (aceswarm_pipeline_decoding{decoding="key-frames"} or 2 * aceswarm_pipeline_decoding{decoding="key-frames-waiting"} or 3 * aceswarm_pipeline_decoding{decoding="all-frames-fallback"} or 4 * aceswarm_pipeline_decoding{decoding="all-frames"}) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

2.text: Key frames only, no frame yet

panels.description: How each stream's ffmpeg decodes the broadcast (aceswarm_pipeline_decoding). With PREVIEW_MODE=keyframes or LOW_CPU_PREVIEWS, while the full stream is copied, it decodes key frames only, which saves CPU. That needs key frames ffmpeg can use: IDR frames, or frames with a recovery point, which some broadcasts never send. Key frames only (green): a frame came of them, so the stream stays this way. Key frames only, no frame yet (yellow): the stream is starting, or its key frames are far apart; after 45 s of data with no frame it switches. Switched to every frame (orange): key frames only gave no frame in time (no key frames ffmpeg can use, or key frames more than about 12 s apart), so the stream decodes every frame from then on, which saves less CPU. It stays so until the stream stops or the transcoder restarts; then it waits again. Every frame (blue): the settings want every frame (PREVIEW_MODE=video), or the full stream is re-encoded, which needs every frame. While no ffmpeg runs for a stream, it shows how its last one decoded; no value while the stream has no pipeline.

panels.title: Full screen output and layout changes
Full screen output

targets.expr: (aceswarm_stream_up * on (stream) max by (stream) (aceswarm_pipeline_full_mode{mode="copy"} + on (stream) 2 * aceswarm_pipeline_full_mode{mode="transcode"})) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.description: What each stream's full screen output does with the video of its broadcast (aceswarm_pipeline_full_mode). Copy (green): the video is H.264, which browsers play, and it is passed on as it is. Transcoding (orange): the video is in another codec, such as HEVC, and is re-encoded to H.264, which costs CPU. Not working (grey): the stream doesn't deliver new frames (aceswarm_stream_up is 0), whatever the reason. Only the full screen output counts here: the tile previews and thumbnails are always encoded anew. The mode belongs to each ffmpeg run, so it follows a broadcast that changes its codec mid-stream (see Source video codec).

panels.title: Source video codec

targets.expr: max by (stream) (aceswarm_pipeline_video_codec{codec="h264"} or 2 * aceswarm_pipeline_video_codec{codec="hevc"} or 3 * aceswarm_pipeline_video_codec{codec="mpeg2video"} or 9 * aceswarm_pipeline_video_codec{codec!~"h264|hevc|mpeg2video"}) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.description: The codec of the video each stream's source carries (aceswarm_pipeline_video_codec): what ffmpeg found, or else what the source's program tables say. H.264 is copied to the full screen output, anything else is re-encoded (see Full screen output). While no ffmpeg runs for a stream, it shows its last run's. No value before a stream's first run, or while neither tells.

panels.title: Layout changes

targets.expr: max by (stream) ((increase(aceswarm_pipeline_layout_changes_total{kind="other"}[$__rate_interval]) > bool 0) or 2 * (increase(aceswarm_pipeline_layout_changes_total{kind="pid"}[$__rate_interval]) > bool 0) or 3 * (increase(aceswarm_pipeline_layout_changes_total{kind="codec"}[$__rate_interval]) > bool 0)) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.description: A mark for each time a stream's broadcast changed its layout mid-stream and ffmpeg followed it (aceswarm_pipeline_layout_changes_total). Codec change (orange): the video changed codec, such as H.264 to HEVC, and a new ffmpeg run took over. PID move (blue): the video moved to another PID. The same ffmpeg run reads on where the streams only moved; a new one takes over where they changed too. Other (grey): something else ffmpeg reads changed, such as the sound, and a new run took over. Tables that change around the streams ffmpeg reads don't count, and neither do the changes of a source that waits to take over. A mark is one step of the graph wide: a minute, more at longer ranges. Changes within one step share a mark, which shows the kind that weighs most; Layout changes in range counts them all. Each one is also marked on Delivering new frames.

panels.title: Layout changes in range
panels.description: How many times each stream's broadcast changed its layout mid-stream in the dashboard's range, and ffmpeg followed it (aceswarm_pipeline_layout_changes_total), most first. Streams without a change are not listed. See Layout changes for what counts.

defaults.noValue: No layout changes in this range

panels.title: Video gap at each layout change
panels.description: How long players got no new video frame at each layout change of a stream (aceswarm_pipeline_layout_change_gap_seconds): from the last frame they got before the change to the first one after it. A point shows once the video came back; a change whose video never came back has none. Changes within one step of the graph (a minute, more at longer ranges) share a point, their average. ffmpeg reports its frames once a second, so a change without a pause shows about 1 s. A new ffmpeg run takes a few seconds to show video; a move the same run reads on over takes less.

panels.title: Recovery attempts per hour
panels.description: Every recovery step taken, whether or not it brought video back (aceswarm_stream_recoveries_total): restart-pipeline, restart-engine, switch-path and failover to a hot standby. A stream that waits for a broadcast that is off keeps trying, so it adds steps here and no recovery. The ones that brought video back are in Recoveries per hour.

panels.title: Peers sending data
panels.description: Peers that sent the stream's engine at least one 16 KiB block of stream data during the last gateway sample, on top of 1/8 of what the engine sent them (which covers the acknowledgements and requests a download sends back). The gateway counts only the engine's traffic with the internet, so it misses peers on the engines' own network, such as a hot standby, and it counts the engine's peers: every stream on a shared engine shows the same.

panels.title: Peer countries
panels.description: Where the peers that sent stream data come from, as the gateway sees the engines' traffic with the internet: each engine's top five countries, counted once per engine however many streams share it.

panels.title: Peers connected
panels.description: Peers the engine reports for each stream's session. They can include other engines of Ace Swarm on the same host, such as a hot standby. There is none while the engine's stats request fails.

panels.title: Peers getting data from us
panels.description: Peers each engine sent stream data to between two gateway samples (at least one 16 KiB block on top of 1/8 of what the peer sent us, which covers the acknowledgements and requests a download sends back), from the gateway's connection table. A stream shows 0 while its engine reports no upload speed, since what it sends its peers then isn't stream data. Only peers the engine connected to itself count: the gateway forwards no inbound ports. Every stream on a shared engine that uploads shows the same peers.

panels.title: Upload speed
panels.description: Upload rate each stream's engine reports.

panels.title: Traffic with each peer in range
panels.description: The data our engines exchanged with each peer in the dashboard's range (aceswarm_engine_peer_bytes_total), by the peer's address and country, with a bar for each direction: down (green) is what the peer sent us, up (blue) what we sent it. The 50 largest, each summed over every engine the peer was a peer of. From the gateway's connection table, so headers and acknowledgements count too, and only the engines' traffic with the internet: a peer on the engines' own network, such as a hot standby, is not there. With streams chosen above: the peers of those streams' own engines (the one each plays from, its standbys and the engines kept after a failed move), and of the shared engine of every path they use, which are the peers of all its streams. Prometheus counts a peer from the second time it sees it, so the first seconds with a new peer are left out, and a peer it saw only once has no bar.

targets.expr: topk(50, sum by (peer, country, direction) (increase(aceswarm_engine_peer_bytes_total{stream=~"$stream",role!="shared"}[$__range]) or increase(aceswarm_engine_peer_bytes_total{role="shared"}[$__range]) * on (path) group_left () max by (path) (max_over_time(aceswarm_stream_path{stream=~"$stream"}[$__range]) or max_over_time(aceswarm_stream_standby{stream=~"$stream"}[$__range]))) > 0)

panels.title: Speed with each peer
panels.description: How fast our engines exchange data with each peer (aceswarm_engine_peer_speed_bytes), by the peer's address and country: the 20 fastest each way at each moment, each summed over the engines it is a peer of. It is what the gateway counted between its last two looks at its connection table (5 seconds by default) at the moment Prometheus collects, so a snapshot and not an average. Above zero: from the peer to us. Below zero: from us to the peer. A peer has no line while nothing moves. From the gateway's connection table, so headers and acknowledgements count too, and only the engines' traffic with the internet: a peer on the engines' own network, such as a hot standby, is not there. With streams chosen above: the peers of those streams' own engines (the one each plays from, its standbys and the engines kept after a failed move), and of the shared engine of every path they use, which are the peers of all its streams.

targets.expr: topk(20, sum by (peer, country) (aceswarm_engine_peer_speed_bytes{stream=~"$stream",role!="shared",direction="down"} or aceswarm_engine_peer_speed_bytes{role="shared",direction="down"} * on (path) group_left () max by (path) (aceswarm_stream_path{stream=~"$stream"} or aceswarm_stream_standby{stream=~"$stream"})))

topk(20, sum by (peer, country) (aceswarm_engine_peer_speed_bytes{stream=~"$stream",role!="shared",direction="up"} or aceswarm_engine_peer_speed_bytes{role="shared",direction="up"} * on (path) group_left () max by (path) (aceswarm_stream_path{stream=~"$stream"} or aceswarm_stream_standby{stream=~"$stream"})))

panels.title: Engine memory
panels.description: Memory used by each engine: a stream's own engines, or a path's shared engine that every stream on the path plays from. One line for each place an engine has, not for each container, so an engine that replaces another continues its line: the stream's name, then what the engine is for (playing, standby, kept after a failed move, or starting) and its network path. The Ace Swarm streams dashboard (linked at the top) shows one stream's engines on their own. An engine that reaches the limit (dashed) is killed and restarted; raise ENGINE_MEMORY_MB, or lower ENGINE_MEMORY_CACHE_MB (set it if it is 0) if it gets close.

targets.expr: max by (stream, role, path) (aceswarm_engine_memory_bytes) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.title: Engine memory, share of the limit

targets.expr: max by (stream, role, path) (aceswarm_engine_memory_bytes / aceswarm_engine_memory_limit_bytes) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.description: Each engine's memory as a share of its limit (aceswarm_engine_memory_bytes over aceswarm_engine_memory_limit_bytes), with the lines of the panel on the left: one for each place an engine has, and one for each path's shared engine. An engine that reaches 100% is killed and restarted.

panels.title: Streams per shared engine
panels.description: With "One engine per path" on, streams on the same network path share one engine. While a replaced engine's streams move to its successor, both show.

panels.title: Shared engine restarts per hour
panels.description: Why shared engines were replaced: the stream someone watched failed (watched), too many of its streams failed at once (failures), every stream on it was failing (all-failed), it stopped answering (unresponsive), or someone pressed Restart (manual).

panels.title: Engine memory cache (estimated)
panels.description: Stream data each engine keeps in its memory cache. Engines don't report it, so this is the engine's memory above its lowest reading (at most 145 MiB, an idle engine), at most the cap (dashed, ENGINE_MEMORY_CACHE_MB). A full cache is normal: the engine then drops its oldest data, and its memory stays flat. Where an idle engine uses less than 145 MiB, a full cache can read a few MiB under the cap. An engine that keeps its cache on disk (ENGINE_CACHE_DIR) shows 0. One line for each place an engine has, as in Engine memory above.

targets.expr: max by (stream, role, path) (aceswarm_engine_memory_cache_bytes) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.title: Engine memory cache, share of the cap
panels.description: How full each engine's memory cache is (estimated, see the panel on the left). Engines without a cap (ENGINE_MEMORY_CACHE_MB=0) and engines that keep their cache on disk (ENGINE_CACHE_DIR) don't show here.

targets.expr: max by (stream, role, path) (aceswarm_engine_memory_cache_bytes / aceswarm_engine_memory_cache_limit_bytes) * on (stream) group_left (name) aceswarm_stream_info{stream=~"$stream"}

panels.title: Engines restarted or removed per hour
panels.description: How many runs of an engine ended, by reason (aceswarm_engine_lifetime_seconds). A run ends when the engine is removed, restarted in its container, or exits. A stream's own engine: moved (the stream plays from another engine now), move-failed (the new engine of a move that failed, at once or after it was kept to try again), standby-removed (a hot standby that failed or is no longer needed), sharing (the stream plays from its path's shared engine now), stopped (the stream was stopped, disabled or deleted), leftover (an engine nothing used, such as one an earlier run of the controller left behind), restart (a recovery step, a restart by hand, or a standby that brought no data), oom-killed (it exceeded its memory limit, ENGINE_MEMORY_MB) and exited (it ended by itself, or was stopped or restarted from outside). A shared engine: replaced (a new engine took its place), idle (no stream used it any more) and unresponsive (it stopped answering), and leftover, oom-killed and exited as above. The table below lists each one.

panels.title: How long engines ran, by reason
panels.description: The runs of engines that ended in the dashboard's range (aceswarm_engine_lifetime_seconds): how many, and how long they lasted, from the engine's start or its last restart until it was removed, restarted or exited. Kind: own for an engine of one stream, shared for a path's shared engine. Average: the mean of those runs. Half ran less than: the median, estimated from the histogram's steps (30 s, 1, 2, 5 and 15 min, 1 and 6 h, 1 day, 1 week, 30 days), so it is rough between two steps. Short runs under restart, oom-killed or exited are engines that keep failing.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (kind, reason, le) (increase(aceswarm_engine_lifetime_seconds_bucket[$__range]))) and on (kind, reason) (sum by (kind, reason) (increase(aceswarm_engine_lifetime_seconds_count[$__range])) > 0)

panels.title: Engines restarted or removed
panels.description: Every time an engine was removed, restarted or exited in the dashboard's range, newest first: the engines of the streams picked above, and with All also the shared engines. An engine's name has its stream's id, or its path for a shared engine; the Ace Swarm streams dashboard has this table for each stream by name. From the controller's log, so it needs the logs data source. What: Removed, Restarted in its container by the controller, or Exited: the engine's process ended, and the container runtime starts it again. Why: moved (the stream plays from another engine now), move-failed (the new engine of a move that failed, at once or after it was kept to try again), standby-removed (a hot standby that failed or is no longer needed), sharing (the stream plays from its path's shared engine now), stopped (the stream was stopped, disabled or deleted), leftover (an engine nothing used, such as one an earlier run of the controller left behind), restart (a recovery step, a restart by hand, or a standby that brought no data), oom-killed (it exceeded its memory limit, ENGINE_MEMORY_MB) and exited (it ended by itself, or was stopped or restarted from outside). A shared engine goes for other reasons: replaced (a new engine took its place), idle (no stream used it any more) and unresponsive (it stopped answering). More: what the controller adds to the reason. Was: what the engine was for when it went (playing, standby, kept, starting, shared or other), on the network path in Path; both are empty for an engine that went within seconds of its start. Ran for: from the engine's start, or its last restart, until then.
